titre: The Geyser That Gave Its Name to All the Others
accroche: In Iceland, a single hot spring gave its name to every geyser in the world. It took two centuries to understand why it erupted.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1810, the Scottish geologist George Steuart Mackenzie observes, in the Haukadalur valley in Iceland, the eruptions of a hot spring that the locals already call Geysir, “the gusher.” The water, calm for long minutes, suddenly starts to churn, then shoots up in a column of boiling water and steam, sometimes several dozen meters high. Back in Scotland, Mackenzie publishes an account of his journey in 1811, in which he offers the first mechanical explanation of what he has just seen: an underground cavity where steam would build up before forcing its way to the surface.

## A Buried Pressure Cooker

Mackenzie's hypothesis is broadly right, and modern science has refined it without overturning it. A geyser requires three conditions: a supply of water, an underground heat source, and above all a conduit that narrows in places. This pressurized plumbing sets it apart from a simple hot spring. Water seeping in comes into contact with rocks heated by the volcanic underground, and rises well beyond 100°C without boiling: the pressure of the water and rock above keeps it liquid, “superheated.” When steam bubbles, accumulating toward the surface, finally force the constriction in the conduit, the pressure drops all at once along the whole column. The superheated water turns to steam almost instantly, over the entire height, and ejects what remains of the liquid water above it: a chain reaction, not a simple push.

## A Name Gone Common

The word geyser enters the English language as early as 1780, drawn from the Icelandic verb geysa, “to gush,” and ever since it has stood on its own for all the geysers of the world, including those that have never heard of their Icelandic namesake. Geysir's own activity, meanwhile, eventually declined: nearly extinct by 1916, revived here and there over the course of the 20th century, it became so irregular that from 1981 on, Icelandic authorities triggered its eruptions on demand, for big occasions, by pouring soap into the conduit. Soap lowers the surface tension of the water and makes it easier for steam bubbles to form, artificially speeding up the same chain reaction. Using soap became rare in the 1990s, out of environmental concern, though the sources do not specify what damage was feared. Two centuries after Mackenzie, the mechanism of the eruption is at last understood with precision; what exactly the soap damaged has never been documented.

repere.texte: In 1846, the German chemist Robert Bunsen measures columns of 45 to 54 meters during eruptions of Iceland's Geysir. In 2000, an earthquake wakes it up: it then reaches 122 meters, for two days, one of the highest columns ever recorded for a geyser.

carte.punch: A single geyser gave its name to all the others, two centuries before anyone understood it.
carte.idee: In Iceland, a hot spring called “the gusher” gave its name to every geyser in the world as early as 1780. It took two centuries of observation, from Mackenzie in 1811 to modern science, to understand that its eruptions are a steam chain reaction, not a simple underground jet.

quiz.question: Why does a geyser erupt all at once, rather than through gradual boiling?
choix: Because the water, as soon as it reaches 100°C at depth, turns entirely and abruptly into steam
Because a geyser accumulates lava at depth, which eventually breaks through the surrounding rock
Because the soap Icelandic authorities used in the past triggers an explosive chemical reaction
Because the pressure in the conduit keeps the water liquid above 100°C, and a pressure drop at a constriction turns it to steam all at once
quiz.explication: In a geyser, the water stays liquid well above 100°C thanks to the pressure in the narrowed conduit. When that pressure gives way at a constriction, it drops all at once along the whole water column, which turns to steam almost instantly: it is this chain-reaction drop, not gradual boiling or a volcanic phenomenon, that throws the water upward. Soap speeds up this same reaction; it does not replace it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who proposes the first mechanical explanation of the Geysir eruption, and in what year?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mackenzie visits Geysir in 1810 and in 1811 publishes the travel account in which he offers the first known mechanical explanation of the eruption: an underground cavity of pressurized steam.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what distinguishes a geyser from a simple hot spring?
choix: Much more intense volcanic activity at depth
A water temperature well above 100°C at the surface
A conduit that narrows in places, putting the water under pressure
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that a geyser requires three conditions, water, underground heat, and above all a conduit that narrows in places, a pressurized plumbing that sets it apart from a simple hot spring.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How high does Geysir's water column reach in 2000, after being revived by an earthquake?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The benchmark states that an earthquake wakes Geysir up in 2000 and that its column then reaches 122 meters for two days, one of the highest ever recorded for a geyser.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do Icelandic authorities pour soap into Geysir's conduit starting in 1981?
choix: To clean the conduit of the mineral deposits clogging it
To lower the water temperature and prevent visitors from being burned
To test a new method of measuring underground pressure
To trigger its eruptions on demand, for big occasions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Geysir's activity became so irregular that from 1981 on, the authorities triggered its eruptions on demand, for big occasions, by pouring soap into the conduit.
